analysis.one_liner: Converts part of Social Security into personal investment accounts while reducing guaranteed benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have enacted the privatization 'Model 2' from President Bush's 2001 Social Security commission, was referred to committee on the day it was introduced in March 2002 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write into law 'Reform Model 2' from the President's Commission to Strengthen Social Security, the December 2001 report commissioned under President Bush. Under that model, workers could divert a portion of their payroll taxes into personal investment accounts, and future guaranteed Social Security benefits would be reduced to help pay for it. Unusually, the bill was introduced by Rep. Robert Matsui, a senior Democrat on Social Security matters, together with the House Democratic leader, the Democratic whip, and the top Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee — yet no Republican cosponsored it, and the committee it went to never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who opt into personal accounts would own investments they could pass to heirs, and the plan's minimum benefit would raise benefits for the lowest earners. The largest structural winner would be the financial industry: diverting a slice of payroll taxes into individual accounts would channel a huge new stream of retirement money through mutual funds and brokerage firms that charge fees on managed assets.

how_it_helps.text: The bill enacts Reform Model 2, which would let workers build personal retirement accounts funded by money now paid into Social Security.
Account balances would be individually owned property, giving workers something to pass on to heirs — a feature current Social Security benefits lack.
The commission model the bill incorporates includes a higher minimum benefit aimed at raising payments for the lowest earners.

analysis.who_pays: Future retirees would bear reduced guaranteed benefits relative to current law, with their retirement income increasingly tied to market performance. During the transition, money diverted from payroll taxes would no longer be available to pay current benefits, so the trust fund shortfall would deepen, requiring new federal borrowing or general revenue — costs ultimately borne by taxpayers. And the plan would also be imposed through a single sentence enacting an entire commission report by reference, with details left to regulations.

drawbacks.text: The bill would supersede the existing Social Security Act to the extent necessary to run the commission's model, replacing a guaranteed, inflation-protected benefit with a system in which part of retirement income depends on individual account returns.

Because payroll tax revenue diverted into accounts could not pay current benefits, the transition would require substantial new federal borrowing or general revenue transfers — a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

The bill contains no policy details at all: it enacts the commission's entire report by reference and delegates everything else to regulations written by the Commissioner of Social Security and the Treasury Secretary, so Congress would be approving a program it had not written out line by line.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside — personal accounts, inheritable balances, and a higher minimum benefit for the poorest retirees — comes entirely at the price of lower guaranteed benefits for future retirees and expensive transition financing that would worsen the program's finances before any savings arrived. The one-sentence enactment of an entire commission report by reference is also poor legislative design. As drafted, the core promise of Social Security would be reduced while a new asset-management revenue stream would be created, so the costs clearly outweigh the benefits for most working people.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled it for action, and it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Matsui introduced the bill on March 20, 2002 'for himself, Mr. Gephardt, Ms. Pelosi, and Mr. Rangel' — the House Democratic leader, the Democratic whip, and the senior Democrat on Ways and Means.

The bill would enact Reform Model 2 as set out in the December 21, 2001 report of the President's Commission to Strengthen Social Security, superseding the Social Security Act and the tax code as needed to operate it.
All three cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on to a bill that would enact a plan produced by a commission appointed under a Republican president.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction and received no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in its record.
The 107th Congress ended January 3, 2003, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries came out ahead: the traditional program's guaranteed benefits were left untouched. The financial firms that would have earned fees managing diverted payroll-tax money did not get that revenue, and the commission's model remained unenacted.

sides.party_line_note: The only supporters were four Democrats (the sponsor and three cosponsors), and no vote was ever held, so the bill's partisan shape was never tested — even though the plan it would enact came from a commission created under a Republican president and every committee action was controlled by Republicans who took none.

industries.industry: Financial services and asset management (mutual funds, brokerages)
industries.note: Model 2 would divert a portion of payroll taxes into individually owned accounts, routing a large new stream of retirement savings through firms that charge fees on managed assets. The accounts would be paid for in part by cutting guaranteed benefits, so the industry's gain comes at the cost of the program's core promise to retirees.

Businesses would continue withholding payroll taxes but the system's rules would change, creating some recordkeeping and administrative adjustment during the transition. The effect on employers is minor compared with the program-level changes.
